meta.title: Who really said "Gratitude is a fruit of great cultivation; you do not find it among gross people"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Johnson: spoken at Dunvegan on 20 September 1773 and printed in Boswell’s Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides (1785), pp. 283–84 — minus its opening ‘Sir’.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Gratitude is a fruit of great cultivation; you do not find it among gross people'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified. Johnson said it at Dunvegan on 20 September 1773; Boswell printed it in the Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides (1785), pp. 283–84 — then disagreed with it.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Johnson said it aloud at Dunvegan on the Isle of Skye on Monday, 20 September 1773, after Boswell remarked that it was hard M’Leod should find ingratitude in so many of his people. James Boswell printed it in The Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides, with Samuel Johnson, LL.D. (London, 1785), pp. 283–84, where the sentence opens “Sir, gratitude is a fruit of great cultivation…” on p. 283 and runs over the page turn to finish on p. 284.

source.heading: Where the line actually appears

docMeta.dd: The Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides, with Samuel Johnson, LL.D.
Monday, 20 September 1773 — Dunvegan, Isle of Skye
London, 1785 — printed by Henry Baldwin for Charles Dilly (pp. 283–84)

source.excerpt: I observed, it was hard that M’Leod should find ingratitude in so many of his people. JOHNSON. ‘Sir, gratitude is a fruit of great cultivation; you do not find it among gross people.’ I doubt of this. Nature seems to have implanted gratitude in all living creatures.
trail: The 1785 London first edition ↗, printed by Henry Baldwin for Charles Dilly, carries the sentence across pages 283–84 in the entry for Monday, 20 September 1773: page 283 ends “you do not find” with the catchword “it”, and page 284 opens “it among gross people.”
Project Gutenberg’s text of the Journal ↗ gives the same reading, including the vocative: “Sir, gratitude is a fruit of great cultivation; you do not find it among gross people.”

Boswell’s original manuscript journal, published by Pottle and Bennett ↗, records it too, punctuated with a full stop: “gratitude is a fruit of great cultivation. You do not find it among gross people.”
Wikiquote ↗ lists it among sourced Johnson quotations, citing the Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides (1785) and the date 20 September 1773 — matching the printed text.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the Project Gutenberg text of Boswell’s revised edition, with spelling modernised; the 1785 first edition reads the same in period orthography. Note the opening “Sir,” and Boswell’s immediate objection — both are cut from the version that circulates.

source.rightsNote: The sentence was first published in Boswell’s Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides (London: Henry Baldwin for Charles Dilly, 1785), far earlier than the 1931 US public-domain cutoff, so Johnson’s words and Boswell’s surrounding narrative are both free of copyright. Modern critical and annotated editions carry their own editorial copyright, but the text quoted here follows the 1785 printing.

author.name: Samuel Johnson
author.heading: Who was Samuel Johnson?
author.bio: Samuel Johnson was an English writer and polymath — poet, essayist, moralist, critic, biographer and, most famously, the compiler of A Dictionary of the English Language (1755). He is quoted more often for his talk than his writing, because James Boswell followed him with a notebook and published what he heard. In 1773 the two toured the Scottish Highlands and Hebrides together; Johnson wrote his own account, A Journey to the Western Islands of Scotland, and Boswell wrote the conversational one that produced this line.

misattribution.heading: The attribution is right — the sourcing usually isn’t
misattribution.intro: This one is genuine Johnson. What goes wrong is everything around it: the book it gets pinned to, the missing first word, and the impression that Johnson wrote it down himself.

items.why: A-Z Quotes cites it to “James Boswell, Samuel Johnson (1786). ‘Boswell’s Life of Johnson: including Boswell’s Journal of a tour of the Hebrides…’, p.264” — a later combined volume. Boswell’s Life of Samuel Johnson was not published until 1791 ↗; the sentence belongs to the separate Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides.

Boswell prints the reply as “Sir, gratitude is a fruit of great cultivation; you do not find it among gross people.” The circulating version silently drops the vocative and capitalises “Gratitude” — a small trim, but it converts a retort into an aphorism. See the passage in the Journal ↗

Johnson never published this. It is talk, taken down by Boswell — and Boswell followed it in print with his own dissent, “I doubt of this. Nature seems to have implanted gratitude in all living creatures.” 1785 first edition, pp. 283–84 ↗
Typical aggregator pages carry the line with the author’s name and nothing else — no work, no date, no page — which is how the wrong-book citations spread unchallenged. Example ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Johnson really said it — at Dunvegan on the Isle of Skye, Monday 20 September 1773, printed by Boswell in the 1785 first edition of the Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides, pages 283–84 ↗.

context.heading: A landlord’s complaint, and a biographer who disagreed
lead: Johnson and Boswell were staying at Dunvegan, the house of the Laird of MacLeod, midway through their 1773 tour of the Hebrides. Over the morning’s talk Johnson had been urging MacLeod to raise his rents and put his idle retainers to productive work; Boswell then observed that it was hard MacLeod should find ingratitude in so many of his people. Johnson’s answer — gratitude is cultivated, not natural — lands as a maxim, but in context it is a landlord’s consolation delivered inside an argument about the collapse of Highland feudal loyalty.

What almost never travels with the quote is that Boswell immediately disagreed with it, in print, in the very next sentence — over the page turn, on p. 284. That dissent is why the line reads so differently in Boswell’s book than it does on a gratitude-journal graphic: it is one side of an argument, not a settled conclusion.
detailsBody: Boswell’s private journal, published from the original manuscript by Frederick A. Pottle and Charles H. Bennett, carries the same sentence with a full stop instead of a semicolon: “Sir,” said he, “gratitude is a fruit of great cultivation. You do not find it among gross people.” The classical authority Boswell reached for next is not a manuscript-versus-print difference at all: the manuscript and the 1785 first edition agree, and both credit the lion mentioned by Valerius Maximus. Boswell corrected it to Aulus Gellius (Noctes Atticae V.14) only in the third edition of 1786 — as Pottle and Bennett note at the line, “Sic in the first edition, but changed to Aulus Gellius in the third, with a reference in a footnote: Aul. Gellius, Lib. v., c. xiv.”

The practical point for anyone quoting it: both the private notebook and the book Boswell published record the sentence, which is unusually strong evidence for an eighteenth-century remark reported in conversation.
